title: Leaf lace scarf
subtitle: A delicate leaf-pattern lace worked flat in fingering-weight yarn.
excerpt: A straight scarf knitted flat in a six-row leaf lace repeat on 3.5 mm needles with fingering-weight yarn. The openwork leaf motif builds from simple yarn-overs and decreases and finishes at 18 cm wide by 170 cm long. Blocking opens the lace to its full width and sets the leaf shapes.
sourceNotes: Leaf lace patterns appear throughout Weldon's Practical Knitter (1880s-1900s), Internet Archive. The leaf motif using yarn-over increases flanked by k2tog and ssk decreases is documented in Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938), citations only.
heroPrompt: A finished leaf lace scarf in pale sage fingering-weight yarn, pinned open on a white blocking mat showing the full leaf motif pattern, natural daylight from one side.

chartDefinition.caption: Chart shows one 12-stitch, 6-row leaf repeat. RS rows read right to left; WS rows read left to right. Repeat chart across body stitches, working 2-stitch garter border at each edge on every row.

glossaryTerms.definition: Wrapping the yarn around the right needle between two stitches to create a new stitch and an eyelet hole. Abbreviated yo in US patterns, yfwd (yarn forward) or yon (yarn over needle) in UK patterns depending on context.
Knit two stitches together as one, forming a right-leaning decrease. One stitch is consumed.
Slip, slip, knit: slip two stitches knitwise one at a time, then knit them together through the back loops, forming a left-leaning decrease.
Soaking the finished piece in cool water, pressing out excess water, and pinning to the stated dimensions on a blocking mat while it dries. Essential for opening lace to its full pattern.
A cast-on that uses the tail and working yarn over two fingers to produce a neat, elastic edge and one row of knitting simultaneously.

content.text: This is a straight scarf knitted flat from one short end to the other in a six-row leaf lace repeat, finishing at 18 cm wide and 170 cm long after blocking. The leaf shapes emerge from paired
yarn-overs
and decreases worked across twelve stitches per repeat, with a two-stitch garter border at each long edge to stop the fabric from rolling.

Flat construction keeps the lace clean: a blocked lace scarf needs no seam that would cut across the pattern. Working back and forth lets you read the chart on RS rows and purl straight across on WS rows. The finished scarf needs about 350 m (around 100 g) of fingering-weight yarn and drapes over the shoulders easily.
What you need

items.name: Fingering-weight yarn, wool or wool-silk blend
items.substitutions: Any fingering-weight yarn. Wool or a wool-silk blend blocks open well and holds the leaf shape. Pure plant fibres block flat but relax once worn.

items.name: 3.5 mm needles, straight or circular (UK 10 / US 4)
items.qty: 1 pair or 1 circular 60 cm or longer
items.substitutions: Go up to 3.75 mm if your tension runs tight.

items.name: Blocking mat and rust-proof pins
items.substitutions: A folded towel works but a rigid mat pins more accurately.

content.text: Gauge

24 sts x 32 rows = 10 x 10 cm in stocking stitch on 3.5 mm needles, blocked. The lace pattern at gauge produces approximately 22 sts per 10 cm across the leaf repeat. Work a 20-stitch swatch over at least 8 cm, block it flat, and measure across the centre once dry. One stitch per 10 cm off gauge changes the finished width by approximately 1 cm: 23 sts per 10 cm gives about 19 cm width; 21 sts per 10 cm gives about 20 cm. Gauge drift across the full 476-row length moves the finished scarf up to 10 cm longer or shorter than stated.
Stitches used
K (knit, US: k): insert right needle from left to right through the front of the stitch, wrap yarn counterclockwise, draw loop through.
P (purl, US: p): insert right needle from right to left through the front of the stitch with yarn in front, wrap yarn counterclockwise, draw loop through to the back.

YO (yarn over, US: yo; UK: yfwd between two knit stitches): bring yarn to the front between the needles, then over the right needle tip to the back before the next knit stitch. Creates one new stitch and one eyelet.
K2tog
(knit two together, US: k2tog): insert the right needle through two stitches at once and knit them together. Right-leaning decrease.
SSK
(slip, slip, knit, US: ssk): slip two stitches knitwise one at a time, return both to the left needle in their new orientation, and knit through the back loops together. Left-leaning decrease.
Pattern
Cast on
Use the
long-tail cast-on

to place 42 stitches on the needle. The stitch count is 3 repeats of 12 sts (36 sts) plus 2 garter border stitches each side (4 sts) = 40 sts, padded to 42 with one extra at each edge for ease of working. Before you start, measure the cast-on tail using the formula: tail_cm = (needle circumference mm x stitch count) / 10 + 15. For 3.5 mm needles (circumference approximately 11 mm) and 42 stitches: (11 x 42) / 10 + 15 = 46.2 + 15 = about 61 cm. Leave a tail of at least 61 cm before making your slip knot.
Stitch count check-in: after the cast-on, count your stitches. You should have 42 stitches on the needle.
Place a stitch marker after stitch 2 and before stitch 41 to mark the 2-stitch garter border at each edge.
Body

The body works the 2-stitch garter border in knit on every row. The 38 centre stitches work the 6-row leaf lace repeat across 3 pattern repeats of 12 stitches (plus 2 selvedge stitches). Work as follows:
Row 1 (RS): K2, slip marker, [K2, SSK, K1, YO, K1, YO, K1, K2tog, K2] 3 times, slip marker, K2. (42 sts)
Row 2 (WS): K2, slip marker, P38, slip marker, K2. (42 sts)
Row 3 (RS): K2, slip marker, [K1, SSK, K1, YO, K3, YO, K1, K2tog, K1] 3 times, slip marker, K2. (42 sts)
Row 4 (WS): K2, slip marker, P38, slip marker, K2. (42 sts)
Row 5 (RS): K2, slip marker, [SSK, K1, YO, K5, YO, K1, K2tog] 3 times, slip marker, K2. (42 sts)
Row 6 (WS): K2, slip marker, P38, slip marker, K2. (42 sts)
Repeat rows 1 to 6 until the scarf measures 170 cm from the cast-on edge, measured along the straight grain. At the halfway mark (approximately row 240, about 85 cm), count your stitches.
Stitch count check-in: at row 240 you should still have 42 stitches on the needle.
Bind off

Work a suspended bind-off on a right-side row: K2, *slip both stitches back to the left needle, K2tog, K1; repeat from * to the last stitch, draw yarn through. This gives a looser, more elastic edge than a standard bind-off, which matters for lace because the bound-off edge must pin open to match the cast-on edge during blocking. If the bound-off edge still feels tight, bind off on a needle one size larger.
Common faults

Stitch count creeping up over several repeats. Each yarn-over must be paired with exactly one decrease in the same row. If you work a yarn-over without its matching decrease, you add a stitch. Check the count at the end of every right-side row, not just at the checkpoints.

Leaf shapes not opening after blocking. This usually means the yarn-overs are being worked too tight. Try lifting the yarn deliberately over the needle rather than pulling it snug. Wet blocking, not steaming, is the correct approach for fingering-weight lace.
Lace looks closed and dense before blocking. That is normal. Fingering-weight lace always looks collapsed until it is pinned out wet. Trust the blocking step.

Bound-off edge pulls inward and shortens one end. This is a too-tight bind-off. Work the bind-off row at deliberately loose tension, or use the needle-up-a-size approach. A tight bind-off on lace can lose 3-4 cm of length after pinning.
Finishing
Weave in the cast-on and cast-off tails along the back of the garter border, changing direction once. Trim close to the fabric.
Wet blocking

is not optional for lace. Soak the finished scarf in cool water for 20 minutes, press out the water gently without wringing, and roll in a clean towel. Pin to a blocking mat at the stated dimensions: 18 cm wide and 170 cm long. Pin the long edges first, then the short ends, easing the leaf shapes open with your fingers. Leave flat overnight to dry completely before removing the pins.
Care

Handwash in cool water with a small amount of wool wash. Support the wet weight of the scarf fully while moving it. Roll in a towel to remove excess water, then pin flat to dry. Do not wring. Lace is fragile when wet because the yarnovers can distort under the weight of the piece.
What to try next

From here the natural step is a longer piece in the same yarn weight. The lace stole works the same leaf motif across a wider cast-on and reaches shawl length. Alternatively, try the mesh lace scarf, which uses a simpler yarn-over grid rather than a shaped motif and is a good first step if this chart felt demanding.
